system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: MCA territory ischemia commonly causes contralateral face-arm weakness and sensory loss greater than leg involvement, with aphasia in dominant hemisphere lesions or neglect in nondominant lesions.
vignette: A right-handed 70-year-old man suddenly develops right facial droop, right arm weakness greater than leg weakness, and nonfluent aphasia.
lead: Which vascular territory is most likely affected?
distractor_notes: ACA infarction causes leg-predominant deficits and abulia more often than aphasia with face-arm weakness.
A right MCA lesion would cause left-sided deficits and may cause neglect rather than dominant-hemisphere aphasia.
PCA infarction commonly causes visual field deficits and memory abnormalities.
Basilar artery disease causes brainstem and posterior circulation findings.
key_expl: Dominant-hemisphere MCA ischemia causes aphasia plus contralateral face-arm-predominant weakness.
objective: Localize a dominant MCA stroke using cortical language and motor findings.
clues: right face-arm weakness greater than leg

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: The ACA supplies medial frontal and parietal cortex, including leg motor-sensory regions and circuits involved in initiation and bladder control.
vignette: A patient has sudden left leg weakness and sensory loss much greater than arm involvement, urinary incontinence, and abulia.
lead: Which cerebral artery is most likely occluded?
distractor_notes: MCA stroke usually affects face and arm more than leg.
A left ACA lesion would cause right leg deficits.
PCA disease primarily affects visual cortex and thalamic/temporal regions.
Basilar artery disease causes brainstem or bilateral posterior circulation deficits.
key_expl: Contralateral leg-predominant deficits plus abulia and urinary dysfunction localize to the ACA territory.
objective: Localize leg-predominant cortical stroke findings to the ACA.

sources.title: Stroke
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes focal neurologic deficits resulting from cerebral arterial occlusion.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Compression of the optic chiasm injures crossing nasal retinal fibers, causing loss of temporal visual fields in both eyes.
vignette: A pituitary macroadenoma compresses the optic chiasm.
lead: Which visual-field defect is most likely?
distractor_notes: A right homonymous hemianopia follows a left retrochiasmal lesion.
Monocular blindness results from optic nerve injury before the chiasm.
Binasal loss is uncommon and does not result from midline chiasmal compression.
Central scotoma is more typical of optic nerve or macular disease.
key_expl: The optic chiasm contains crossing nasal retinal fibers that carry temporal visual fields.
objective: Predict visual-field loss from optic chiasm compression.

sources.title: Pituitary tumors
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes pituitary tumors as causing visual problems when they compress nearby optic pathways.

sources.title: Pituitary Tumors
sources.support: NINDS describes visual-field deficits from pituitary mass effects.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: A lesion posterior to the optic chiasm affects fibers representing the same contralateral visual hemifield from both eyes.
vignette: A stroke damages the left optic tract.
distractor_notes: Monocular blindness results from prechiasmal optic nerve injury.
Bitemporal loss results from chiasmal injury.
A left optic tract lesion affects the right visual field, not the left.
A central scotoma is not the typical tract-level defect.
key_expl: Left retrochiasmal lesions cause loss of the right visual hemifield in both eyes.
objective: Localize homonymous visual-field loss to the contralateral retrochiasmal pathway.

sources.title: Visual Field Test
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes visual-field testing for pathway lesions.

sources.title: Stroke
sources.support: NINDS describes visual-field loss as a cortical or retrochiasmal stroke manifestation.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Cortical alpha-synuclein pathology causes fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and spontaneous parkinsonism.
vignette: A 73-year-old man has progressive cognitive decline with marked day-to-day fluctuations, recurrent formed visual hallucinations, and new rigidity and bradykinesia.
distractor_notes: Alzheimer disease usually begins with steadily progressive episodic memory impairment and lacks early prominent hallucinations and parkinsonism.
Frontotemporal dementia often begins with behavior or language changes at a younger age.
Vascular dementia is associated with cerebrovascular injury and often a stepwise course.
Normal aging does not cause hallucinations, parkinsonism, or major functional cognitive decline.
key_expl: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, and spontaneous parkinsonism strongly suggest Lewy body dementia.
objective: Differentiate Lewy body dementia from Alzheimer and other dementias.

sources.title: Lewy body dementia
sources.support: NIA describes cognitive fluctuations, visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, and parkinsonism in Lewy body dementia.

sources.title: Lewy body dementia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes dementia with Lewy bodies and its characteristic cognitive and movement symptoms.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Degeneration of frontal and anterior temporal lobes causes early personality, behavioral, executive, or language dysfunction with relatively preserved memory early in disease.
vignette: A 56-year-old executive becomes socially disinhibited, apathetic, and compulsive over 2 years while episodic memory remains relatively preserved.
lead: Which brain regions are most likely undergoing predominant degeneration?
distractors: Posterior columns of the spinal cord
distractor_notes: Occipital disease primarily affects vision.
Cerebellar disease causes ataxia.
Primary motor cortex degeneration alone causes motor deficits rather than behavioral disinhibition.
Posterior column disease affects proprioception and vibration.
key_expl: Early behavioral and executive change with relative memory preservation points to frontotemporal degeneration.
objective: Link behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia to frontal/anterior temporal degeneration.

sources.title: Frontotemporal disorders
sources.support: NIA describes frontal and temporal lobe degeneration causing behavior and language changes.

sources.title: Frontotemporal dementia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes frontotemporal dementia as degeneration affecting behavior, personality, and language.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Median nerve compression at carpal tunnel
mechanism: Compression of the median nerve beneath the transverse carpal ligament causes sensory symptoms in the lateral 3.5 digits and weakness/atrophy of thenar muscles.
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has nocturnal numbness of the thumb, index, and middle fingers with thenar weakness.
distractor_notes: Ulnar neuropathy affects the medial hand and intrinsic hand muscles.
Radial neuropathy affects wrist/finger extension and dorsal hand sensation.
Musculocutaneous nerve supplies elbow flexors and lateral forearm sensation.
Axillary nerve supplies deltoid and lateral shoulder sensation.
key_expl: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median nerve compression producing lateral digit paresthesias and thenar weakness.
objective: Localize carpal tunnel syndrome to the median nerve.

sources.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes median nerve compression causing hand numbness and weakness.

sources.title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
sources.support: NINDS describes median nerve compression beneath the transverse carpal ligament.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Ulnar nerve compression near the medial epicondyle impairs interossei and medial hand sensation, causing weak finger abduction/adduction and numbness of the fifth digit.
vignette: A cyclist develops numbness in the fifth digit and weakness spreading the fingers apart.
lead: Which nerve is most likely affected?
distractor_notes: Median nerve injury affects thenar muscles and lateral digits.
Radial nerve injury affects extension.
Axillary nerve affects shoulder abduction.
Femoral nerve supplies the anterior thigh and quadriceps.
key_expl: Interossei are innervated by the ulnar nerve, which also supplies the fifth digit.
objective: Localize hand intrinsic weakness and fifth-digit numbness to the ulnar nerve.

sources.support: MedlinePlus describes ulnar neuropathy causing numbness in the ring/little fingers and hand weakness.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Cluster headache is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia causing brief, excruciating unilateral orbital pain with ipsilateral lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and restlessness in stereotyped clusters.
vignette: A 32-year-old man has severe 45-minute attacks of unilateral orbital pain occurring nightly for 3 weeks, with ipsilateral tearing and nasal congestion. He paces during attacks.
distractor_notes: Migraine lasts longer, often causes nausea/photophobia, and patients usually prefer rest in a dark room.
Tension headache is bilateral pressing pain without autonomic features.
Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock facial pain lasting seconds.
Temporal arteritis occurs in older adults and causes scalp tenderness and systemic inflammation.
key_expl: Short, severe unilateral orbital attacks with autonomic symptoms and restlessness occurring in clusters are classic cluster headache.
objective: Differentiate cluster headache from migraine and trigeminal neuralgia.

sources.title: Cluster headache
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes severe unilateral orbital pain with tearing and nasal symptoms in recurring clusters.

sources.title: Headache
sources.support: NINDS describes cluster headache as a trigeminal autonomic headache disorder with stereotyped severe attacks.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Cortical spreading depolarization is implicated in migraine aura and produces transient positive and negative neurologic symptoms that typically evolve over minutes before headache.
vignette: A 27-year-old woman sees expanding zigzag lines for 20 minutes before a throbbing unilateral headache with photophobia.
lead: Which process most directly underlies the visual aura?
distractor_notes: Retinal embolization causes sudden negative monocular visual loss rather than a gradually spreading binocular positive phenomenon.
Occipital seizures are usually much briefer and not the typical migraine aura mechanism.
Optic neuritis causes painful monocular vision loss.
Angle closure causes ocular pain and pressure with halos.
key_expl: Migraine aura is linked to a propagating wave of cortical depolarization and altered neural activity.
objective: Connect gradually evolving visual aura to cortical spreading depolarization.

sources.title: Migraine
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes migraine aura as transient visual or neurologic symptoms preceding headache.

sources.title: Migraine
sources.support: NINDS describes cortical spreading depolarization as an important mechanism associated with migraine aura.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin-producing neurons destabilizes sleep-wake regulation and causes excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations.
vignette: A 21-year-old woman has irresistible daytime sleep attacks and sudden episodes of muscle weakness triggered by laughter while consciousness is preserved.
lead: Loss of which hypothalamic neuropeptide is most strongly associated with this disorder?
distractor_notes: Dopamine modulates alertness and movement but is not the defining deficient peptide in narcolepsy type 1.
GABA is broadly inhibitory but not selectively lost in narcolepsy.
Oxytocin mediates reproductive and social functions.
Vasopressin regulates water balance and circadian signaling but is not the defining deficit.
key_expl: Narcolepsy with cataplexy is strongly associated with loss of orexin-producing hypothalamic neurons.
objective: Relate cataplexy and sleep attacks to orexin deficiency.

sources.title: Narcolepsy
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hallucinations in narcolepsy.

sources.title: Narcolepsy
sources.support: NINDS describes hypocretin/orexin deficiency as central to narcolepsy with cataplexy.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Major depressive disorder is defined by at least 2 weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest plus associated cognitive, vegetative, and psychomotor symptoms causing impairment, without mania.
vignette: A 38-year-old woman has 6 weeks of depressed mood, loss of interest, early-morning awakening, low energy, poor concentration, guilt, and reduced appetite. She has never had mania or hypomania.
distractor_notes: Persistent depressive disorder requires a chronic duration measured in years rather than this discrete major episode.
Bipolar I disorder requires a manic episode.
Adjustment disorder requires symptoms tied to a stressor without meeting criteria for another disorder; this patient meets a major depressive syndrome.
Normal grief does not typically produce a sustained pervasive syndrome with the full symptom cluster and functional impairment.
key_expl: A ≥2-week episode with depressed mood/anhedonia and multiple neurovegetative-cognitive symptoms, without mania, is major depressive disorder.
objective: Recognize major depressive disorder from duration, symptom count, and absence of mania.

sources.title: Depression
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes major depression as persistent mood and functional symptoms lasting at least two weeks.

sources.support: NIMH describes diagnostic symptoms and duration of major depressive episodes.
